claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains at least two chemically and electrochemically distinct phases, exemplified as BCC and FCC phases.
The alloy develops a thin in-situ protective oxide film at elevated temperature.
The proposed exposure combines sliding wear with a chloride-containing oxidizing environment at approximately 800 °C.
Phase boundaries and oxide-film integrity are the structural mediators of coupled degradation.
Micro-galvanic coupling occurs between the distinct eutectic phases at their boundaries.
The BCC phase is anodic relative to the cathodic FCC phase.
The protective oxide layer forms primarily on the more cathodic FCC phase.
Sliding wear mechanically removes the protective oxide scale.
Removal of the oxide exposes fresh, electrochemically active surfaces, particularly on the anodic BCC phase.
The exposed phases and electrochemical gradients create localized micro-galvanic cells that promote anodic dissolution and localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion at phase boundaries weakens the structure and exacerbates wear.
Oxide removal increases wear by reducing friction protection and structural integrity.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, total degradation will be significantly greater than the arithmetic sum of wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
The simultaneous-exposure wear track will be deeper than under wear-only conditions because of recurrent oxide-scale removal.
The anodic phase will corrode faster under simultaneous exposure than under static corrosion-only exposure because galvanic interactions are intensified.
The mutually reinforcing wear and corrosion processes will accelerate overall mass loss.
The proposed controlled comparison uses wear-only, corrosion-only, and simultaneous wear-corrosion groups at the same temperature.
Persistence of an uninterrupted protective oxide film despite wear would falsify the proposed oxide-removal mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires total degradation to exceed the arithmetic sum while comparing wear depth and corrosion rate to their respective single-exposure controls. The falsification rule instead suggests that mass loss, wear depth, and corrosion rate must each exceed the sum of the individual tests, which is a stronger and partly dimensionally ill-defined requirement.
